cards.text: Job just asked his friends why the wicked live on, growing old and increasing in power (Job 21:7). Now Eliphaz the Temanite, one of Job's three friends (Job 2:11), answers him. He opens with questions: “Can a man be of use to God? Can even a wise man benefit Him?”

cards.question: Eliphaz asks Job, “Does it delight the Almighty that you are righteous?” Then he asks if God profits when Job's ways are blameless. True or false: Eliphaz is saying God profits from Job's goodness.

cards.text: Then Eliphaz asks, “Is it for your reverence that He rebukes you and enters into judgment against you?” Translation: friend, God is NOT taking you to court for being too holy.

cards.question: So Eliphaz rules out Job's reverence as the reason for his trouble. What does Eliphaz say the reason is instead?

cards.text: Now Eliphaz stops asking and starts LISTING: he says Job needlessly demanded security from his brothers and took the clothing of the naked. Friend, I spent YEARS in a junk drawer and nobody ever wrote me up like this.

cards.question: Next on Eliphaz's list are the weary and the famished. What does he claim Job did to them?

answers.text: Charged them for water and food
Sent them away to another town

cards.text: Eliphaz adds that this happened “while the land belonged to a mighty man, and a man of honor lived on it.” Remember, this is the man the Bible introduces as blameless and upright (Job 1:1).

cards.question: Eliphaz's list keeps going. He says Job sent ___ away empty-handed, and the strength of the ___ was crushed.

cards.text: Then comes the big word. Eliphaz says, “Therefore snares surround you, and sudden peril terrifies you,” which is a fancy way of saying, Job, you did this.

cards.question: Eliphaz says it is so dark around Job that he cannot see. What else does Eliphaz say covers Job?

cards.text: Now Eliphaz points UP: “Is not God as high as the heavens? Look at the highest stars, how lofty they are!” My boy Berry would've had his face pressed to the window for this one.

cards.question: After pointing to how high God is, Eliphaz tells Job what Job supposedly says about Him. True or false: Eliphaz claims Job says thick clouds keep God from seeing us.

cards.text: Eliphaz asks, “Will you stay on the ancient path that wicked men have trod?” Those men were snatched away before their time, and their foundations were swept away by a flood.

cards.question: Eliphaz says those wicked men of old were snatched away before their time. What does he say they told God?
True or false: Eliphaz says it was God who filled the houses of those wicked men with good things.

cards.text: Then Eliphaz says, “so I stay far from the counsel of the wicked.” Friend, that's JOB'S line, word for word (Job 21:16), and that's like somebody quoting your own text back to you in the group chat.

cards.question: Eliphaz says that when the wicked are destroyed, the righteous see it and are ___.

cards.text: And in Eliphaz's picture, the innocent mock the wicked: “Surely our foes are destroyed, and fire has consumed their excess.”

After the whole LIST, Eliphaz turns around and hands Job an invitation: “Reconcile now and be at peace with Him; thereby good will come to you.” That's like your boss chewing you out for an hour and then sliding you a cookie.

cards.question: Eliphaz tells Job to receive instruction from God's mouth. Where does Eliphaz say Job should lay up God's words?
True or false: Eliphaz promises Job that if he returns to the Almighty, he will be restored.

cards.text: Eliphaz adds: remove injustice from your tents, and send your gold to the dust, even the gold of Ophir to the stones of the ravines. Not the everyday gold, friend, the OPHIR gold.

cards.question: If Job lets go of his gold, what does Eliphaz say will be his gold and his finest silver?

cards.text: Then, Eliphaz says, Job will delight in the Almighty and lift up his face to God. I think Eliphaz is painting Job a whole comeback story here.

cards.question: True or false: Eliphaz says that even if Job prays to God, God will stay silent.
Earlier, Eliphaz said it was so dark around Job that he could not see. Now he promises that Job's decisions will be carried out and ___ will shine on his ways.

cards.text: Eliphaz even says Job's words could help others: “When men are brought low and you say, ‘Lift them up!’ then He will save the lowly.”

cards.question: Eliphaz ends by saying God could rescue someone through the cleanness of Job's hands. Who does he say God could deliver that way?

answers.text: Even one who is not innocent

cards.text: Grab your apron, friend, because Job's story is FAR from done.

findings.problem: Right after quoting v8 about 'a mighty man' and 'a man of honor,' the card says 'Remember, this is the man the Bible introduces as blameless and upright (Job 1:1).' 'This is the man' can be read as naming the mighty man of v8 as Job. The text leaves open who v8 describes and how it connects to the charges, so the card should not point to it this way.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The card says Eliphaz's line is 'JOB'S line, word for word (Job 21:16).' The joke then compares it to 'somebody quoting your own text back to you,' which presents it as Eliphaz deliberately throwing Job's words back at him. The text never says Eliphaz is quoting Job, so this adds a connection and a reason that neither passage states. The claim that the wording is an exact match also has to be confirmed against the BSB of Job 21:16, which is not in the provided text.

rule.text: When he connects two passages, or explains what a law was for, he says only what the texts state.

findings.problem: 'Not the everyday gold, friend, the OPHIR gold' presents Ophir gold as a premium kind of gold as if that were a fact. The passage doesn't say so, and the card gives no reference.

rule.text: **References.** Every Bible fact he states carries its reference.

findings.problem: The card says Job's words 'could help others.' Verse 29 is a firm promise: 'then He will save the lowly.' Changing 'will' to 'could' turns the promise into a possibility.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The question says 'God could rescue someone' and 'Who does he say God could deliver.' Verse 30 says 'He will deliver... rescuing him,' a definite promise, not a possibility.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The last story card is only the 'story isn't over' line and tells no verse, but it cites Job 22:30. Verse 30 is already cited by the choice card before it. The citation rule ties a story card's verses to what it tells, and this card tells nothing.
findings.question: When a last story card is only the 'story isn't over' line (allowed when the last verse is asked on a choice card), what should its "verses" field cite: the last verse of the passage, the whole stop, or something else?

findings.problem: Most cards are plain retelling with no real laugh. Examples are stop 1 cards 1, 13 and 18, and stop 2 cards 6 and 9. Only a few cards try for a laugh: stop 1 cards 5, 11 and 16, and stop 2 card 1. Several of these lines read like a pleasant narrator, not Papa Dorin's laugh-out-loud voice.

rule.text: When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
